   Shopee and Lazada remove fake storefronts ahead of 11.11 sale
 Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox
 Both platforms confirmed that they have taken enforcement measures against the counterfeit stores.
 PHOTO: LIANHE ZAOBAO
 Andy Ng
 Published   Nov 11, 2026, 04:30 PM
 Updated   Nov 11, 2026, 05:51 PM
 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise 中文 Shopee and Lazada removed at least 20 fake storefronts before the 11.11 sale. Both said they banned accounts and tightened checks to protect shoppers.
 A Lianhe Zaobao probe found at least 10 fake stores on each platform. They copied names, logos and colours of big retailers, and used fake five-star reviews.
 Experts warned shoppers to check URLs and report suspicious listings. Singapore police said scams caused $410.6 million in losses in the first half of 2026.
 AI generated
 SINGAPORE – E-commerce giants Shopee and Lazada have removed at least 20 fake online storefronts impersonating reputable retailers on their platforms, ahead of the 11.11 shopping sale on Nov 11.
 Both companies confirmed that they have taken enforcement measures against the counterfeit stores, reported Chinese-language daily Lianhe Zaobao.
 In response to queries from The Straits Times, a Shopee spokesperson said that the reported listings have been removed and the fake seller accounts banned.
 “Listings or shops that infringe intellectual property rights are prohibited on our platform,” the spokesperson said.
 Shopee uses both manual and automated measures to detect and remove non-compliant listings, and is constantly refining its tools to identify storefronts that mimic established brand names and their logos, the spokesperson added.
 According to Zaobao, one of the stores used a green logo that is very similar to that of pharmaceutical chain Watsons, thereby misleading consumers into thinking that it is the official Watsons store.
 “Shopee is committed to protecting consumers and maintaining a trusted environment for online commerce,” said the company.
 “We take reports seriously and encourage users to report suspicious listings through the in-app ‘Report this Product’ function, so that our team can take appropriate action. We remain committed to strengthening our enforcement processes and supporting a safe, reliable shopping experience for all users.”
 A Lazada spokesperson told ST that the company takes reports of potentially fraudulent or misleading online stores seriously, and has tightened measures ahead of 11.11 to ensure “a safe and trusted shopping experience for our customers”.
 The measures, including taking down stores identified to have violated Lazada’s policies, have resulted in a decline in suspicious brand impersonation stores, the spokesperson added.
 “We have established seller onboarding and verification processes, alongside ongoing monitoring for suspicious seller activity or listings that may violate our platform policies,” Lazada said.
 “Where potential violations are identified, we review the relevant seller accounts and listings and take action... which may include removing listings or suspending or banning sellers.”
 The statement added: “We encourage customers to report any suspicious activity or concerns. We will continue to strengthen our safeguards to protect customers and brand partners, and uphold trust in our marketplace.”
 The move by both platforms follows a two-week investigation by Zaobao, which uncovered at least 10 fraudulent stores on each platform.
 According to the Chinese daily, the fake sellers misappropriated the names, logos, and signature brand colours of “prominent department stores, malls, supermarkets, and drugstores across Singapore and Malaysia”.
 Some fraudulently labelled themselves “official stores” to lure shoppers with branded cosmetics, perfumes, and skincare products discounted to under 20% of their original retail prices.
 To fabricate legitimacy, the storefronts displayed numerous five-star reviews.
 However, a closer look by a Zaobao reporter revealed recurring review-farming tactics: identical user profiles repeatedly posted five-star ratings across various products within the same shop, often accompanied by photos featuring near-identical backgrounds and product arrangements.
 Both Shopee and Lazada have urged consumers to remain vigilant and report suspicious listings directly through their apps.
 In an advisory e-mail on Nov 10, DBS Bank said shoppers should be wary of unusually low prices, check seller reviews and use secure payment options rather than transferring money directly, as scammers may use a tempting deal to lure victims without honouring purchases made.
 The bank also urged people not to click on suspicious links or scan QR codes sent by unknown persons or companies.
 They should instead verify payment and delivery requests directly through official apps or websites.
 This is because such phishing links disguised as payment or delivery websites may help scammers steal banking credentials, card details or one-time passwords (OTPs) for unauthorised transactions.
 Shoppers are also advised not to download potentially malicious apps through links or QR codes provided by unknown sellers.
 Apps should only be installed via official app stores, and the operating systems and security software of devices should be kept updated, said DBS.

 Originally started at China’s Nanjing University in 1993 as “Bachelor’s Day” – a counter to Valentine’s Day when single people gathered, partied and bought gifts for themselves – Singles’ Day has transformed into what is now known as “the world’s largest online shopping festival”.
 Now spanning several weeks of massive retail discounts, the event outscales both Black Friday and Cyber Monday in global sales, according to global financial website Investopedia.
 However, experts also said that shoppers should be wary of fake websites that spoof recognised or popular sites during such popular shopping festivals.
 Consumers Association of Singapore president Melvin Yong previously told ST : “Beware of fake websites by carefully checking URLs for misspellings, odd characters or suspicious domain extensions, as scammers often create deceptive sites resembling legitimate ones.”
 In releasing the mid-year scam statistics on Aug 26, the Singapore Police Force said $410.6 million was lost in scams in the first six months of 2026, compared with $500.2 million during the same period in 2025.
 They also warned that scams remain the dominant crime type in Singapore.
